title: What is the difference between a classic `switch` statement (colon syntax, fall-through, needs `break`) and a `switch` expression (arrow syntax, `yield`, no fall-through, exhaustiveness), which types can a `switch` operate on, and why is `switch(null)` a classic NPE before pattern-matching switch?
shortTitle: What is the difference between a switch statement and a switch expression, which types can switch operate on, and why is switch(null) a classic NPE?
topicTitle: What is the difference between a classic `switch` statement

s1_definition.profdef: The classic `switch` statement uses colon-style `case X:` labels, falls through from one case into the next unless you write `break`, and does not return a value. The modern `switch` expression (standardized in Java 14) uses arrow-style `case X ->` labels, does not fall through, can produce a value directly, uses `yield` to return a value from a block arm, and when it switches over an `enum` or sealed type the compiler enforces exhaustiveness so every possibility is handled. A traditional `switch` operates on `int`, `char`, `byte`, `short` and their wrappers, on `String`, and on `enum`; modern Java also allows pattern-matching switches over object types and sealed hierarchies. Passing `null` to a classic non-pattern switch throws `NullPointerException` because the switch tries to unbox or dereference the selector.
s1_definition.analogy: Think of Rajesh walking up to a bank counter sorted by service type. The old `switch` statement is like a row of connected counters where, if you do not put up a "stop" sign (break) after finishing at counter DEPOSIT, you accidentally slide into counter WITHDRAW and get served there too — that accidental sliding is fall-through. The new `switch` expression is like modern separate counters: you go to exactly one, get your token, and leave, and the manager even checks that there is a counter for every service type so nothing is missed. And if you walk up with no service type at all (null), the old system crashes because it cannot figure out which counter you want.
s1_definition.oneliner: The classic switch falls through and needs `break`; the arrow switch expression returns a value, never falls through, and is checked for exhaustiveness.
s1_definition.raw:
**Professional definition:** The classic `switch` statement uses colon-style `case X:` labels, falls through from one case into the next unless you write `break`, and does not return a value. The modern `switch` expression (standardized in Java 14) uses arrow-style `case X ->` labels, does not fall through, can produce a value directly, uses `yield` to return a value from a block arm, and when it switches over an `enum` or sealed type the compiler enforces exhaustiveness so every possibility is handled. A traditional `switch` operates on `int`, `char`, `byte`, `short` and their wrappers, on `String`, and on `enum`; modern Java also allows pattern-matching switches over object types and sealed hierarchies. Passing `null` to a classic non-pattern switch throws `NullPointerException` because the switch tries to unbox or dereference the selector.

**In simple words (banking analogy):** Think of Rajesh walking up to a bank counter sorted by service type. The old `switch` statement is like a row of connected counters where, if you do not put up a "stop" sign (break) after finishing at counter DEPOSIT, you accidentally slide into counter WITHDRAW and get served there too — that accidental sliding is fall-through. The new `switch` expression is like modern separate counters: you go to exactly one, get your token, and leave, and the manager even checks that there is a counter for every service type so nothing is missed. And if you walk up with no service type at all (null), the old system crashes because it cannot figure out which counter you want.

**One line to remember:** The classic switch falls through and needs `break`; the arrow switch expression returns a value, never falls through, and is checked for exhaustiveness.

sections.s2_technical:
The classic switch statement looks like this. `switch (type) { case "DEPOSIT": handleDeposit(); break; case "WITHDRAW": handleWithdraw(); break; default: reject(); }`. The crucial behavior is fall-through: if you forget `break` after the DEPOSIT case, execution continues into WITHDRAW. Sometimes fall-through is intentional, for example grouping cases: `case "SAVINGS": case "CURRENT": applyInterestRules(); break;` where both account types share the same handler.

The switch expression uses arrows and produces a value. For example `String tier = switch (balanceBand) { case LOW -> "BRONZE"; case MID -> "SILVER"; case HIGH -> "GOLD"; };`. Each arm handles exactly one label with no fall-through, so no `break` is needed. If an arm needs several statements, you use a block and `yield` the value: `case HIGH -> { audit(); yield "GOLD"; }`. The `yield` keyword returns a value out of a switch-expression block, which is different from `return` that would exit the whole method.

Exhaustiveness is a big improvement. When a switch expression switches over an `enum`, the compiler requires that every enum constant is handled or that a `default` arm exists. This means if someone later adds a new enum constant, the code fails to compile until the new case is handled, which catches a whole class of bugs at compile time instead of in production. For example, if `AccountType` is an enum and you add `NRI`, a switch expression without a default will refuse to compile until you handle `NRI`.

Which types can a switch operate on. Historically: `byte`, `short`, `char`, `int` and their wrappers `Byte`, `Short`, `Character`, `Integer`, plus `String` (since Java 7), plus any `enum`. It cannot switch on `long`, `float`, `double`, or `boolean`. Modern pattern-matching switch (Java 21) can switch on any reference type and match type patterns, like `case Savings s ->` and `case Current c ->`, and can include a `null` case explicitly.

The `switch(null)` trap: in a classic switch over a `String` or a wrapper or an `enum`, if the selector is `null`, the switch tries to compute a hash or unbox the value to choose a branch, and because the value is null this throws `NullPointerException` before any case is considered — the `default` arm does NOT catch it. The only way a switch can handle null is the modern pattern-matching switch with an explicit `case null ->`. So in older code you must null-check before the switch. A senior nuance is that a switch expression must be exhaustive, which is why switch expressions over sealed types are so powerful: the compiler proves you covered every permitted subtype.
sections.s3_banking:
National Bank of India routes incoming payment instructions by their type: a DEPOSIT credits an account, a WITHDRAW debits it, a TRANSFER moves money between two accounts, and anything else must be rejected. The routing logic was originally written as an old-style switch and it had two real production bugs that we will reproduce and then fix.

Problem 1 — a developer forgot a `break` after the WITHDRAW case, so a withdrawal accidentally fell through into the TRANSFER code and attempted a transfer with a missing destination account, corrupting a ledger entry. This is exactly the fall-through hazard of the classic switch statement.

Problem 2 — a null payment type arrived from a buggy upstream system, and the classic switch over the type String threw a NullPointerException that crashed the whole batch instead of cleanly rejecting the one bad message. This is exactly the `switch(null)` trap.

The fix converts the routing to a modern switch expression. The arrow arms cannot fall through, which removes the missing-break bug class entirely, and the method returns a routing decision value directly. We keep an explicit null guard before the switch to reject null cleanly, and we show how a switch expression over an enum of account tiers is exhaustive so adding a new tier forces a compile error until it is handled.

The code defines an `Account`, a `PaymentInstruction`, an `AccountTier` enum, and a `PaymentRouterService`. The service has a `route` method that uses a switch expression to decide the action, and a `classifyTier` method that uses an exhaustive switch expression over the enum. The demo runs a deposit, a withdrawal, a transfer, and a null type to show clean rejection.

sections.s5_journey:
Input data: five payment instructions with types DEPOSIT, WITHDRAW, TRANSFER, GIFT, and null, plus a tier classification for Rajesh who is HIGH.

Step 1. The DEPOSIT instruction enters `route`. The type is not null, so control reaches the switch expression. The arm `case "DEPOSIT"` matches and the expression yields "CREDIT SAV2001". There is no fall-through, so execution leaves the switch immediately with that value.

Step 2. The WITHDRAW instruction matches `case "WITHDRAW"` and yields "DEBIT CUR3001". In the old statement style, a missing break here could have fallen into TRANSFER; the arrow form makes that impossible.

Step 3. The TRANSFER instruction matches the block arm. Inside the block, the from id SAV2001 and to id CUR3001 are read, then `yield` returns "MOVE SAV2001->CUR3001". The yield returns a value from the switch arm, not from the whole method.

Step 4. The GIFT instruction matches no named case, so the `default` arm yields "REJECTED_UNKNOWN".

Step 5. The null instruction is caught by the explicit null guard before the switch, which logs a warning and returns "REJECTED_NULL_TYPE". No NullPointerException occurs because the switch is never reached with a null selector.

Step 6. The tier classification for HIGH enters the enum switch expression, matches `case HIGH`, and yields "GOLD". Because every enum constant is handled, the compiler accepted this switch with no default.

Final output:

```
2026-10-30 18:22:10 [INFO] Route DEPOSIT  -> CREDIT SAV2001
2026-10-30 18:22:10 [INFO] Route WITHDRAW -> DEBIT CUR3001
2026-10-30 18:22:10 [INFO] Route TRANSFER -> MOVE SAV2001->CUR3001
2026-10-30 18:22:10 [INFO] Route UNKNOWN  -> REJECTED_UNKNOWN
2026-10-30 18:22:10 [WARNING] Null payment type — rejecting cleanly (no NPE).
2026-10-30 18:22:10 [INFO] Route null     -> REJECTED_NULL_TYPE
2026-10-30 18:22:10 [INFO] Tier label HIGH -> GOLD
```

```
  Input: PaymentInstruction(type, from, to, amount)
    │
    ▼
  PaymentRouterService.route(inst)
    │
    ├─ type == null ? ──── yes ──→ log WARNING ──→ return "REJECTED_NULL_TYPE"
    │        │ no
    │        ▼
    │   switch EXPRESSION (arrow arms, no fall-through)
    │        │
    │        ├─ "DEPOSIT"  -> "CREDIT " + fromId
    │        ├─ "WITHDRAW" -> "DEBIT " + fromId
    │        ├─ "TRANSFER" -> { read ids; yield "MOVE a->b"; }
    │        └─ default    -> "REJECTED_UNKNOWN"
    │
    ▼
  returned routing decision (a value)

  classifyTier(AccountTier) → exhaustive switch over enum
    LOW→BRONZE  MID→SILVER  HIGH→GOLD   (compiler proves all covered)
```

sections.s6_takeaway:
The classic switch statement uses colon-style case labels, it falls through from one case into the next unless you write an explicit break, and it does not produce a value. The modern switch expression, standardized in Java 14, uses arrow-style case labels, it never falls through, it can produce a value directly, and inside a multi-statement arm you use yield to return the value of that arm. When a switch expression switches over an enum or a sealed type, the compiler enforces exhaustiveness, meaning every possibility must be handled, which turns a whole class of missed-case bugs into compile-time errors.

On which types a switch can operate, the traditional switch works on byte, short, char, int and their wrapper types, on String since Java 7, and on any enum. It cannot switch on long, float, double, or boolean. Modern pattern-matching switch in Java 21 extends this to any reference type with type patterns and even allows an explicit null case.

The switch-on-null trap is one I have hit in production. In a classic switch over a String or a wrapper or an enum, if the selector is null, the switch tries to unbox or hash the value to pick a branch and throws a NullPointerException before any case runs, and crucially the default arm does not catch it. The only switch that can handle null natively is the pattern-matching switch with an explicit null case. So in ordinary code I always null-check before the switch.

In our payment routing service at National Bank of India, the original code was an old-style switch and it had two real bugs. A missing break after the withdraw case fell through into the transfer logic and corrupted a ledger entry, and a null payment type from a buggy upstream threw a NullPointerException that killed the whole batch. I rewrote the routing as a switch expression, which made fall-through impossible and removed the missing-break bug class entirely, and I added an explicit null guard so a null type is rejected cleanly as one bad message instead of crashing the batch. I also used an exhaustive switch expression over our account-tier enum so that if anyone adds a new tier, the code will not compile until they handle it, which protects us at build time rather than in production.
